boardStatus.primaryBoard: American Board of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery (ABOHNS), primary certification in Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery.
boardStatus.status: ABOHNS is the relevant US primary specialty certifying board for the prerequisite specialty surrounding rhinology. ABOHNS lists nose/sinus diseases in primary otolaryngology scope and, as checked 2026-10-07, identifies its subspecialty subcertifications as Complex Pediatric Otolaryngology, Neurotology and Sleep Medicine. It does not list a rhinology subcertification or separate rhinology board examination. The American Rhinologic Society is a professional society, not a board certifier.
boardStatus.blueprintScope: No publicly published stand-alone rhinology exam blueprint or domain weightings were found. The curriculum is mapped pedagogically to publicly described ABOHNS primary assessment areas—basic science/physiology/pathophysiology, patient care, data gathering and interpretation, diagnosis, non-surgical management and surgical management—and to the board’s broad nose/sinus scope. This is not an official ABOHNS blueprint, endorsement, question bank, eligibility determination or exam predictor.
boardStatus.fellowshipAccreditation: The MEE and Harvard fellowship pages establish an institutional clinical fellowship and its broad goals, but do not state that this specific rhinology fellowship is ACGME-accredited. ACGME’s current OTO-HNS materials list Neurotology and Pediatric Otolaryngology subspecialty standards, not a rhinology accreditation standard. Accreditation status of the MEE fellowship is therefore not asserted.

boardEligibilityNotice: This independent course cannot establish ABOHNS eligibility, MEE fellowship eligibility, ACGME completion/accreditation, a qualifying prior residency, medical licensure, supervised experience/case volume, clinical or procedural competence, or certification. Rhinology has no separate ABOHNS subcertification/board exam listed as of 2026-10-07. Consult MEE, ACGME and ABOHNS directly for current programme/accreditation/eligibility facts.

boardStatus: Institutional clinical physician fellowship, not a distinct ABOG subspecialty board. ABOG board subspecialty page was dynamic and its text could not be fetched; public ABOG search results enumerate five subspecialties and exclude global women’s health. This is an evidence-limited negative finding, date checked 2026-10-07; recheck ABOG directly before relying on it.
boardEligibilityNotice: BWH states applicants must complete a four-year ACGME-approved OB/GYN residency and be eligible for Massachusetts medical licensure; fellowship participation/degree does not itself confer ABOG eligibility, certification, licensure, or an independent specialty credential. Verify individual credential status with ABOG and current program.

boardStatus: No separate ABMS/ABOG subspecialty board certificate titled Complex Benign Gynecology (CBG) was identified in the current ABMS certificate list. ABOG states it offers voluntary MIGS and Pediatric and Adolescent Gynecology Focused Practice Designations. The ABOG MIGS FPD examination is distinct from an independent CBG board certification; current application/exam eligibility, case-log rules and fees must be checked in ABOG’s live bulletin. AAGL accredits CBGF programs; the BWH program sheet listed accreditation period 2022–2026 and the AAGL 2026 CBG listing includes Brigham. Renewal beyond the listed period was not verified.
boardEligibilityNotice: This educational course provides no medical degree, ACGME/AAGL fellowship credit, board eligibility, board preparation guarantee, license, privileges, procedural competence or certification. Real CBGF entry requires completion of obstetrics/gynecology residency per AAGL program requirements; ABOG primary board and FPD eligibility are controlled solely by ABOG’s current rules.
